claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type nanofilms or nanoribbons have a fine-grained microstructure.
The controlled intervention is incremental annealing from 300 °C to 700 °C in a controlled atmosphere with fixed dwell times.
Annealing in the proposed temperature range will relax lattice strain in FeMnNiGeSi-type nanofilms or nanoribbons.
Annealing in the proposed temperature range will cause moderate grain and magnetic-domain coarsening.
Microstructural relaxation and coarsening will reduce domain-wall pinning sites.
Reducing defects and constrained interfacial strain lowers the energy barriers for domain-wall motion.
Lower barriers to domain-wall motion increase magnetocaloric reversibility.
Annealing will increase the isothermal entropy change by no more than approximately 10–15% relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will reduce magnetic hysteresis by approximately 20–30% relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The predicted entropy-change increase and hysteresis reduction will improve low-field cooling efficiency.
Relative to annealed specimens, the as-deposited baseline has a higher defect density.
Relative to annealed specimens, the as-deposited baseline has smaller domains and stronger domain-wall pinning.
Measurements are to be conducted near room temperature under applied magnetic fields of 1–2 T.
The proposed behavior applies to films or ribbons thicker than approximately 20 nm.
The proposed behavior applies for annealing temperatures no higher than 700 °C and magnetic fields no higher than approximately 2 T.
Thermal equilibration limits practical cooling-cycle frequencies in these thin geometries to below approximately 10 Hz.
Below 20 nm, increased interfacial effects may counteract the benefits of annealing and degrade magnetocaloric performance.
Above 10 Hz, heat-transfer limitations may degrade magnetocaloric performance.
The proposed experiment compares specimens annealed for 1 hour at designated temperatures from 300 °C to 700 °C against as-deposited control specimens.
Failure to observe either reduced hysteresis or improved reversible magnetocaloric properties at every tested annealing temperature would refute the proposed annealing mechanism.
